cards.subject: SPF
says: publishes in a DNS TXT record the servers allowed to send for a domain
checks the envelope sender domain rather than the visible From address
stops working for a forwarded message unless the forwarder rewrites the sender
cards.use: need to list which servers may send mail for your domain
not: signs each message with a private key

cards.subject: DKIM
says: signs selected headers and the body of each message with a private key
publishes the matching public key in DNS so receivers can verify the signature
fails verification when something alters the signed body in transit
cards.use: need receivers to confirm a message was not changed after it left your system
not: lists the IP addresses allowed to send for the domain

cards.subject: DMARC
says: tells receivers what to do with mail that fails authentication for the visible From domain
asks receivers to send reports about mail claiming to be from your domain
builds on SPF and DKIM rather than replacing them
cards.use: need to instruct receivers how to treat spoofed mail and see who is sending as you
not: encrypts the message body between servers

cards.subject: A DKIM selector
says: lets one domain publish several DKIM public keys side by side
appears as the s= tag in the DKIM-Signature header
makes key rotation possible without breaking mail already in flight
cards.use: need to rotate a signing key without a gap in valid signatures
not: names the receiving mail server

cards.subject: DMARC p=none
says: asks receivers to take no action on failing mail but still send reports
is the usual starting point when first publishing a DMARC record
cards.use: are publishing DMARC for the first time and want to see who sends as you before enforcing
not: blocks all mail from the domain

cards.subject: DMARC p=quarantine
says: asks receivers to treat failing mail as suspicious, typically by placing it in spam
sits between monitoring only and outright refusal
cards.use: have fixed your legitimate senders and want failing mail sent to spam first
not: asks receivers to ignore the record

cards.subject: DMARC p=reject
says: asks receivers to refuse mail that fails DMARC at delivery time
is the strongest enforcement setting and the most effective against spoofing the domain
cards.use: have confirmed every legitimate sender passes and want spoofed mail refused outright
not: is safe to switch on before checking third-party senders

cards.subject: The Return-Path address
says: receives bounce messages for a delivery
is the envelope sender domain that SPF is evaluated against
can differ from the visible From address when a provider sends on your behalf
cards.use: need to know where bounces go and which domain SPF checks
not: is the address shown to the reader in the inbox list

cards.subject: DMARC alignment
says: requires the SPF or DKIM authenticated domain to match the visible From domain
can pass through either aligned SPF or aligned DKIM
cards.use: see SPF pass yet DMARC fail because a provider's bounce domain differs from your From domain
not: is satisfied by any passing SPF result regardless of domain

cards.subject: A DMARC aggregate report
says: is an XML summary of mail seen claiming to be from your domain
shows which sending sources passed or failed SPF and DKIM
is sent to the address named in the rua tag
cards.use: need to discover forgotten systems that send mail as your domain
not: contains the full text of each rejected message

cards.subject: MTA-STS
says: tells sending servers to require TLS when delivering to your domain
is published as a DNS record plus a policy file served over HTTPS
cards.use: want sending servers to refuse to downgrade delivery to your domain to plain text
not: signs outgoing messages with a private key

cards.subject: A verified sender
says: proves to a provider that you control an address or domain before it will send as you
is required by many providers before any mail goes out
cards.use: set up a new sending provider and it refuses to send from your address
not: is the person who approves marketing copy

cards.subject: Sender reputation
says: is a mailbox provider's running judgement of how trustworthy a sender is
is built from bounces, complaints, spam trap hits and authentication results
attaches to both the sending domain and the sending IP address
cards.use: want to understand why good mail suddenly lands in spam
not: is a score you buy from the provider

cards.subject: A hard bounce
says: is a permanent delivery failure such as a mailbox that does not exist
should lead to the address being suppressed immediately
cards.use: see a reply saying the recipient address does not exist
not: clears up on its own after a retry

cards.subject: A soft bounce
says: is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a busy receiving server
is retried for a while before the address is treated as failing
cards.use: see a deferral because the recipient's mailbox is full
not: means the address will never accept mail

cards.subject: A spam complaint
says: happens when a recipient marks your message as spam
is reported back by some mailbox providers through a feedback loop
damages reputation more than an ordinary unsubscribe does
cards.use: want to know why people clicking the spam button hurts you more than leaving quietly
not: is a bounce sent by the receiving server

cards.subject: A feedback loop
says: forwards complaint reports from a mailbox provider to the sender
lets the sender remove complaining recipients from future mail
cards.use: need to learn which recipients reported your mail as spam
not: reports DNS errors in the SPF record

cards.subject: A suppression list
says: stores addresses that must never be mailed again
is checked before every send
holds hard bounces, complainers and unsubscribes
cards.use: need a guarantee that a bounced or unsubscribed address is never mailed again
not: is the list of people who opened the last campaign

cards.subject: IP warm-up
says: raises sending volume gradually so mailbox providers learn the sender's pattern
starts with the most engaged recipients
cards.use: move to a brand new sending IP and must send a large volume
not: means sending the entire list on the first day

cards.subject: A dedicated IP
says: gives one sender sole ownership of the reputation of its IP address
needs steady volume to build and keep a good reputation
cards.use: send enough steady volume to justify controlling your own reputation
not: removes the need for SPF and DKIM

cards.subject: A shared IP
says: pools reputation among many senders using the same address
can be harmed by another customer's bad behaviour
cards.use: send low or irregular volume and cannot build a reputation alone
not: gives you exclusive control of its reputation

cards.subject: A spam trap
says: is an address real people never use or an abandoned one reused to catch bad list practices
signals that a list was bought, scraped or never cleaned
cards.use: see a sudden reputation drop after importing an old purchased list
not: is a folder where spam is delivered for inspection

cards.subject: List hygiene
says: removes invalid and long-inactive addresses on a regular schedule
protects reputation by lowering bounce and trap hits
cards.use: want to lower bounces before a large campaign
not: adds new addresses from purchased lists

cards.subject: Domain separation
says: sends marketing and transactional mail from different subdomains or streams
stops a marketing complaint spike from blocking password resets
cards.use: fear that a campaign problem could block receipts and security alerts
not: means using one address for all mail so reputation is shared

cards.subject: Transactional email
says: is triggered by a user's own action or account event
is expected by the recipient and does not need marketing consent
must arrive promptly and reliably
cards.use: send a receipt, password reset or order confirmation
not: is bulk mail promoting a new product

cards.subject: Marketing email
says: promotes products, offers or news to a list
requires consent and a working unsubscribe
is judged by engagement and complaint rates
cards.use: want to announce a new feature to everyone who opted in
not: is sent only after a user changes their password

cards.subject: A password reset email
says: contains a single-use link that expires quickly
is sent with a neutral on-screen confirmation whether or not the address has an account
cards.use: build the flow that lets a locked-out user regain access
not: includes the user's current password for convenience

cards.subject: A receipt email
says: confirms a completed purchase with the amount and a reference
serves as a record the customer may need later
cards.use: must give a customer proof of a payment
not: advertises unrelated products as its main content

cards.subject: A security alert
says: warns about activity such as a new sign-in or a changed credential
tells the recipient how to secure the account if it was not them
is sent even to users who unsubscribed from marketing
cards.use: detect a sign-in from a new device
not: is optional and skipped when the user mutes notifications

cards.subject: A deadline alert
says: warns that a date is approaching before a penalty or expiry
is useful only if sent early enough to act on
cards.use: must remind a customer about an approaching filing or payment date
not: thanks the customer after a purchase

cards.subject: A drip campaign
says: sends a planned sequence of messages spaced over time
is triggered by an event such as signing up
stops for a person who has completed the goal
cards.use: want to guide new users through the first week with timed messages
not: sends one message to everyone at the same moment

cards.subject: An autoresponder
says: replies automatically to an incoming message or sign-up
confirms receipt but does not promise a human answer
cards.use: want people to know their message arrived
not: is a person writing a personal reply

cards.subject: An out-of-office reply
says: tells senders that the recipient is away and when they return
should be sent only once per sender to avoid reply loops
is marked as automatic so other systems do not answer it
cards.use: are away and want people to know who covers for you
not: should be sent for every message from the same sender

cards.subject: A template placeholder
says: is a named slot filled with real data at send time
keeps wording in one place while names and numbers vary
cards.use: need one message design to carry each person's name and invoice number
not: is a hard-coded value typed into every message

cards.subject: Output escaping
says: converts markup characters in user data into harmless text
stops a name containing HTML from injecting content into the message
cards.use: insert a customer-supplied name into an HTML email
not: removes the need to validate the recipient address

cards.subject: A default value
says: supplies fallback text when a variable is missing
prevents a message from reading Hello , with a blank name
cards.use: know some records have no first name
not: hides the failure by skipping the send

cards.subject: A shared layout
says: wraps many templates in the same header, footer and styling
lets a legal footer be fixed in one file
cards.use: want every message to carry the same footer and brand styling
not: is a separate copy of each template per language

cards.subject: Template versioning
says: records which template revision produced each sent message
lets support reproduce what a customer actually received
cards.use: need to prove exactly what wording a customer saw last month
not: overwrites old wording so history is lost

cards.subject: A locale-specific template
says: selects wording, date and number formats for the recipient's language
falls back to a default language when a translation is missing
cards.use: serve customers in several languages
not: translates by running the English text through a regex

cards.subject: A sample-data preview
says: renders a template with realistic fake data before it is sent
catches broken placeholders and long names that break layout
cards.use: want a non-developer to check wording before release
not: sends the template to real customers as a test

cards.subject: Header injection protection
says: rejects line breaks in values placed into subjects and recipient headers
stops an attacker adding extra headers or recipients through a form field
cards.use: let users type a value that ends up in a subject line or Reply-To
not: escapes angle brackets in the message body only

cards.subject: A digest
says: batches several related events into one message
lowers volume for events that are not urgent
cards.use: have many low-urgency updates for one person in a day
not: sends each event instantly

cards.subject: A threshold alert
says: fires when a measure crosses a set level instead of on every change
can use several graded levels so the warning comes before the limit is hit
cards.use: want to warn a customer before they run out of an allowance
not: fires on every single change

cards.subject: An actionable message
says: says what happened, what the person should do and who to contact
lets the reader act without searching elsewhere
cards.use: want a message that reduces follow-up tickets
not: only states that something happened

cards.subject: Quiet hours
says: hold non-urgent notifications during a person's rest period
let urgent security messages through
cards.use: want to avoid waking users for low-priority updates
not: delay every message including security alerts

cards.subject: Notification severity levels
says: rank messages so urgent ones use faster, louder channels
decide which messages can be batched and which cannot
cards.use: must decide whether an event warrants SMS or only an in-app badge
not: are the same for every event

cards.subject: Alert deduplication
says: collapses repeats of the same underlying problem into one alert
uses a key such as the resource and condition
cards.use: see the same failure generate hundreds of messages
not: deletes alerts without recording them

cards.subject: An escalation path
says: moves an unacknowledged alert to a second person or channel after a wait
prevents a critical alert from dying in one unread inbox
cards.use: need a critical alert to reach someone who is not responding
not: resends the alert to the same person forever

cards.subject: Notification fatigue
says: occurs when frequent low-value messages train people to ignore all of them
is a failure of volume and relevance rather than delivery
cards.use: notice users disable every notification after a noisy week
not: is cured by sending more reminders

cards.subject: A per-thread mute
says: silences notifications for one conversation while leaving others active
is a user preference applied before a notification is queued
cards.use: want users to stop alerts for one busy conversation only
not: turns off all notifications for the account

cards.subject: An aggregated unread count
says: shows one total of unread items across conversations
is an in-app signal that avoids sending an email for each message
cards.use: want a badge that tells a user how much is waiting
not: is sent to the user by SMS every minute

cards.subject: Opt-in consent
says: records that a person agreed to receive a kind of message
is given by an action such as ticking an unticked box
cards.use: collect addresses for a newsletter
not: is assumed because an address was found online

cards.subject: Double opt-in
says: sends a confirmation link and subscribes only after it is clicked
proves the address belongs to the person who signed up
reduces typos and spam trap addresses on a list
cards.use: must be sure an address is real and owned by the subscriber
not: subscribes the address before any confirmation

cards.subject: An unsubscribe link
says: is a visible link in marketing mail that ends future messages
must work without logging in or paying
cards.use: send marketing mail and need to let people leave easily
not: is hidden in tiny grey text to discourage use

cards.subject: The List-Unsubscribe header
says: lets mail clients show their own unsubscribe button
carries a mailto or https address for the request
cards.use: want Gmail-style clients to offer a native unsubscribe control
not: is displayed in the body of the message

cards.subject: One-click unsubscribe
says: lets a client unsubscribe the user with a single POST request
is signalled by a List-Unsubscribe-Post header
needs no confirmation page for the user
cards.use: must support bulk-sender requirements for easy opt-out
not: requires the user to log in first

cards.subject: A preference center
says: lets people choose topics and frequency instead of leaving entirely
reduces full unsubscribes by offering a lighter option
cards.use: want to keep a subscriber who only dislikes the frequency
not: removes the address from every list at once

cards.subject: A consent record
says: stores who agreed, to what, when and through which form
is evidence if consent is ever questioned
cards.use: must prove a person agreed to receive marketing
not: is a screenshot kept on a laptop

cards.subject: The STOP keyword
says: lets an SMS recipient opt out by replying with a single word
must be honoured by ending further marketing texts to that number
cards.use: send marketing text messages
not: is ignored if the person opted in earlier

cards.subject: A transactional exemption
says: allows service messages without marketing consent
does not cover promotional content added to a service message
cards.use: are tempted to add a discount banner to a receipt
not: lets you send promotions to anyone who bought once

cards.subject: The outbox pattern
says: stores the message in your own database before any delivery attempt
lets a worker deliver it later
avoids losing the message if the process crashes between saving and sending
cards.use: want a send to survive a provider outage or a crash
not: calls the provider inline and ignores the failure

cards.subject: A retry with backoff
says: waits longer between attempts after each failure
avoids hammering a provider that is already struggling
cards.use: keep failing against a provider that is slow
not: retries instantly in a tight loop

cards.subject: Jitter
says: adds randomness to retry delays
stops many clients retrying at the same instant
cards.use: see retries from many workers arriving in synchronised waves
not: makes the retry delay constant

cards.subject: A dead state
says: marks an item as given up after a set number of failed attempts
puts the item in front of a person instead of retrying forever
cards.use: need failures to be visible rather than silent loops
not: deletes the item to keep the queue short

cards.subject: An idempotency key
says: identifies one logical send so a repeat does it only once
protects against duplicates when a request or event is retried
cards.use: fear a retry will email the same customer twice
not: is regenerated on every retry attempt

cards.subject: At-least-once delivery
says: guarantees a message is delivered one or more times
means receivers must tolerate duplicates
cards.use: design a queue that never loses a message
not: promises that no duplicate can ever occur

cards.subject: Provider rate limits
says: cap how many messages a provider accepts in a period
answer excess requests with a rate-limit error that should trigger a slower retry
cards.use: see rejections when a burst of mail is submitted
not: are removed by retrying faster

cards.subject: A token bucket
says: allows short bursts up to its capacity while refilling at a steady rate
spends one token per message sent
cards.use: want to permit a burst but cap the sustained sending speed
not: blocks every request after the first minute

cards.subject: Queue depth
says: counts messages waiting to be sent
rising steadily signals that sending is slower than creation
cards.use: want an early sign that delivery is backing up
not: measures how many recipients opened the mail

cards.subject: A priority queue
says: lets urgent messages overtake bulk ones
keeps password resets from waiting behind a newsletter
cards.use: must send a security code while a large campaign is running
not: sends in strict arrival order whatever the type

cards.subject: Per-domain throttling
says: limits how fast mail goes to each receiving domain
follows the pace a mailbox provider tolerates
cards.use: get temporary deferrals from one large mailbox provider during a campaign
not: sends everything to one domain at once to finish sooner

cards.subject: A circuit breaker
says: stops calls to a failing provider for a cool-off period
lets queued mail wait or switch to a fallback route
cards.use: keep a failing provider from slowing every worker
not: retries each message more aggressively

cards.subject: An in-app notification
says: appears inside the product while the person uses it
suits low-urgency news that can wait until the next visit
cards.use: have a minor update that does not need to reach someone outside the product
not: reaches users who never open the app

cards.subject: Email
says: reaches people outside the product and leaves a durable record
carries long content and attachments
can sit unread for days
cards.use: need a record the customer can keep and search
not: is guaranteed to be read within seconds

cards.subject: SMS
says: reaches a phone without an app or internet data
is short and has per-message cost
is best kept for time-sensitive or verification messages
cards.use: need a short message to cut through, such as a delivery code
not: suits long documents with attachments

cards.subject: A push notification
says: is delivered to an installed app through the platform's service
can be switched off by the user in device settings
cards.use: want an immediate alert to people who installed your app
not: works for people without the app installed

cards.subject: A voice call
says: is a high-intrusion channel for the most critical alerts
suits events needing immediate human attention
cards.use: have an outage alert nobody has acknowledged by other channels
not: is the right default for routine updates

cards.subject: A status page
says: publishes incident updates for everyone at one address
reduces repeated individual enquiries during an outage
cards.use: face an outage with many customers asking the same question
not: is a private message to one customer

cards.subject: Channel fallback
says: moves to a second channel when the first fails or is not read in time
is chosen by the severity of the message
cards.use: need a time-limited approval to reach someone who ignores email
not: sends every channel at once for all messages

cards.subject: An email log record
says: stores recipient, template, time and delivery status for each message
lets support answer where a message went
cards.use: get a ticket saying a customer never received a message
not: stores the full unredacted body of every message forever

cards.subject: A provider message id
says: identifies a message at the provider
links later webhook events back to the original send
can be used to deduplicate repeated events
cards.use: need to match a bounce event to the record you created
not: is the same for every message in a campaign

cards.subject: A delivery status lifecycle
says: moves a message through states such as queued, sent, delivered and bounced
is updated by events reported back from the provider
cards.use: need to show support whether a message is waiting or failed
not: is one flag set true when the send function returns

cards.subject: An audit trail
says: records who was notified, when and why
is append-only so history cannot be quietly edited
cards.use: must show an auditor that a legal notice was sent
not: is rewritten whenever a status changes

cards.subject: Redaction in logs
says: masks personal data and secrets before they are stored
keeps tokens and full addresses out of long-lived logs
cards.use: log enough to debug without storing reset links
not: writes the whole message body to the log

cards.subject: Log retention
says: sets how long delivery records are kept before deletion
balances support and audit needs against privacy
cards.use: decide how long to keep records of sent messages
not: keeps everything forever by default

cards.subject: A correlation id
says: ties together log lines from several services for one request
follows a notification from the triggering action through to the send
cards.use: trace why one action produced no email
not: is the address of the recipient

cards.subject: A dead item review
says: has a person inspect messages that exhausted their retries
looks for patterns such as one bad template or one failing provider
cards.use: see the dead count growing
not: clears the queue without reading it

cards.subject: A plain-text part
says: carries the message as text without markup
is shown by clients that cannot or will not render HTML
lowers the chance of being flagged as spam when it matches the HTML
cards.use: want the message to read in any client and on a watch
not: is optional and can contain different wording than the HTML

cards.subject: An HTML part
says: carries the styled version of the message
needs inline styles and simple structure to render across clients
cards.use: want a branded layout with images and buttons
not: can safely use any modern web layout feature

cards.subject: multipart/alternative
says: packages the text and HTML versions of one message together
lets the client choose which version to display
cards.use: send both a text and an HTML version in one email
not: attaches the files to the message

cards.subject: Inline CSS
says: places style rules on each element instead of in a shared stylesheet
survives clients that strip or ignore head styles
cards.use: see styles disappear in a webmail client
not: relies on external stylesheet links

cards.subject: Table layout
says: uses nested tables for structure because email clients render them predictably
avoids reliance on newer layout features that some clients ignore
cards.use: need a multi-column email that renders in older clients
not: uses CSS grid for all structure

cards.subject: Preheader text
says: is the snippet shown after the subject in the inbox list
can be hidden in the body so it does not appear twice
cards.use: want to control the line of preview text next to the subject
not: is the name shown as the sender

cards.subject: A subject line
says: is the first line a recipient reads in the inbox
should say plainly what the message is about
cards.use: need people to understand the message before opening
not: works best when written in capital letters

cards.subject: A reply-to address
says: is where replies go when it differs from the sender
can send answers to a monitored team inbox
cards.use: send from a system address but want answers to reach support
not: is where bounce messages are delivered

cards.subject: A tracking pixel
says: is a tiny remote image that signals an open when loaded
makes open counts unreliable because clients may preload images
cards.use: need to explain why open rates are an unreliable measure
not: measures clicks on links

cards.subject: Link tracking
says: rewrites links through a redirect so clicks can be counted
can hurt trust when the visible and real link domains differ
cards.use: want to count clicks on a campaign link
not: counts how many times the message was opened

cards.subject: Image blocking
says: hides remote images until the reader allows them
is why alt text and a text fallback matter
cards.use: find that key information inside an image is missing for many readers
not: is switched off in every client by default

cards.subject: Alt text
says: describes an image for screen readers and when images are blocked
should be empty for a purely decorative image
cards.use: include an image that carries meaning
not: is the file name of the image

cards.subject: Descriptive link text
says: says where a link goes or what it does
avoids click here as the only link label
cards.use: let a screen reader user pick links from a list
not: repeats the full URL as the label

cards.subject: Colour contrast
says: makes text readable against its background
is checked with a contrast ratio against a standard
cards.use: use light grey text on white for a footer
not: is satisfied by any two different colours

cards.subject: Not relying on colour alone
says: adds a text label or icon next to colour cues
helps readers who cannot tell the colours apart
cards.use: mark an overdue amount in red
not: uses red for errors and nothing else

cards.subject: Semantic headings
says: use real heading elements instead of bold styled text
let screen reader users move through sections
cards.use: structure a long newsletter so it can be skimmed by assistive technology
not: are chosen by size so the visual look matches

cards.subject: A language attribute
says: tells assistive technology which language to pronounce
prevents a screen reader reading text with the wrong accent
cards.use: send a message in a language different from the reader's default
not: is needed only for right-to-left scripts

cards.subject: Presentation role on layout tables
says: tells assistive technology a table is only for layout
stops a screen reader announcing rows and columns
cards.use: use a table to position a header and footer
not: is needed for real data tables

cards.subject: Touch target size
says: gives buttons enough height and spacing to tap accurately
helps people with limited dexterity and everyone on a small screen
cards.use: design a button that readers will tap on a phone
not: is solved by shrinking the button text

cards.subject: An image-only email
says: leaves the message unreadable when images are blocked or a screen reader is used
often scores worse with spam filters
cards.use: are given a design supplied as one large picture
not: is the most accessible way to keep fonts exact

cards.subject: Plain language
says: uses short sentences and common words
helps readers with limited time, cognitive load or a second language
cards.use: write a message many people will read on a phone while busy
not: uses internal jargon to sound precise

cards.subject: Sandbox mode
says: accepts send requests but does not deliver to real recipients
lets you test integration code without sending live mail
cards.use: want to check the send code without emailing customers
not: delivers mail to a small percentage of real customers

cards.subject: A local mail catcher
says: receives outgoing mail on a local port and shows it in a web page
never forwards the message to the real recipient
cards.use: develop locally and want to see the real rendered email
not: delivers the message through the production provider

cards.subject: A recipient allow-list
says: limits non-production sends to approved addresses or domains
protects real customers from test mail
cards.use: run a staging copy that holds real customer data
not: lets any address receive staging mail

cards.subject: Provider test credentials
says: keep test sends separate from the live account's reputation
are distinct keys from the production ones
cards.use: need a CI job to exercise the send path safely
not: reuse the production API key to save setup

cards.subject: A seed list
says: is a set of test mailboxes at major providers used to check inbox placement
shows whether a campaign lands in inbox or spam before the main send
cards.use: want to see where a campaign lands before the full send
not: is the list of subscribers who clicked last time

cards.subject: A client rendering test
says: shows how a message appears across mail clients and devices
finds broken layouts in dark mode and with images blocked
cards.use: must confirm a template looks right in many clients
not: only needs a look in one browser

cards.subject: A spam score check
says: analyses content and headers for features filters dislike
flags problems such as a missing plain-text part
cards.use: want to catch spam-like content before sending
not: guarantees inbox placement when it passes

cards.subject: A webhook contract test
says: checks that your handler copes with the provider's real event payloads
catches a changed field before it breaks production
cards.use: fear a provider change will break event handling
not: replays the same payload against the live recipient list

cards.subject: A failure-path test
says: simulates bounces, timeouts and rate-limit errors
proves that retries, the dead state and suppression behave
cards.use: want to know the queue copes when the provider is down
not: tests only the success case

cards.subject: A staged rollout
says: sends a new template or flow to a small share first
limits the damage if something is wrong
cards.use: change a high-volume template and fear a rendering bug
not: sends to everyone at once to gain feedback quickly

cards.subject: Leading with the outcome
says: puts the result or required action at the top of the message
lets a busy reader act without reading the rest
cards.use: write to a customer who needs to know what to do by Friday
not: opens with a long company introduction

cards.subject: Naming the next step
says: tells the reader exactly what to do and by when
includes a single clear route to do it
cards.use: want fewer reply-and-ask follow-ups
not: leaves it to the customer to guess

cards.subject: A specific apology
says: names what went wrong and its effect on the customer
states what is being done to fix it
cards.use: must apologise after a billing error
not: says sorry for any inconvenience this may have caused

cards.subject: Avoiding blame
says: describes what happened without accusing the customer or a named colleague
keeps the focus on the fix
cards.use: write after a customer mistake caused the problem
not: points out that the customer should have read the terms

cards.subject: An honest timeline
says: gives a realistic time or says when the next update will come
avoids promising a fix time you cannot control
cards.use: cannot say when an outage will end
not: promises one hour to calm people down

cards.subject: An incident update cadence
says: promises updates at set intervals even when there is nothing new
stops customers chasing for news
cards.use: run a long outage with many customers waiting
not: goes silent until the fix is complete

cards.subject: False urgency
says: pressures the reader with deadlines that do not exist
erodes trust and trains people to ignore genuine urgent messages
cards.use: are tempted to write ACT NOW on a routine reminder
not: raises response rates with no cost

cards.subject: A reply-able sender
says: lets customers answer a message to reach a person or a monitored inbox
shows a human or team name rather than a dead address
cards.use: want customers to feel they can respond
not: uses a no-reply address that discards answers

cards.subject: A consistent voice
says: keeps tone, terms and sign-off the same across emails, app text and support
comes from a short style guide shared by writers and developers
cards.use: find that error text and emails sound like different companies
not: leaves each team to decide its own tone

cards.subject: The Moksy ChatOutbox
says: is the model that stores each recipient notification before delivery
has a server-side drain that sends the stored items
retries items with backoff
cards.use: need to know how the Moksy communications service protects notifications from provider outages
not: calls the provider inline for each message

cards.subject: The Moksy dead state
says: is reached after 6 failed attempts
puts the item in front of a person instead of retrying forever
cards.use: are asked when a Moksy outbox item stops being retried
not: is reached after the first failure

cards.subject: Moksy delivery status persistence
says: keeps delivery status in the database so it survives a restart
stops status being lost when a server process is replaced
cards.use: ask whether delivery status is lost when the Moksy server restarts
not: stores the status only in process memory

cards.subject: The Moksy inbound webhook shared secret
says: guards the inbound webhook routes against callers who lack the secret
sits alongside Twilio signature validation
cards.use: need to know how Moksy keeps strangers off its inbound webhook routes
not: leaves the routes open since the URL is hard to guess

cards.subject: Twilio signature validation
says: checks that an inbound SMS request really came from Twilio
rejects requests whose signature does not match
cards.use: need to know how Moksy verifies inbound text message callbacks
not: trusts any request that contains a valid-looking phone number
like: The Moksy inbound webhook shared secret

cards.subject: The Moksy WebhookEvent model
says: records inbound email and SMS events by provider message id
ensures each event is processed once even when the provider retries
cards.use: need to know how Moksy avoids processing a repeated inbound event twice
not: processes every received event again

cards.subject: Moksy per-user rate limiters
says: cap message, attachment and thread-create routes per user
exempt system and admin senders
cards.use: ask how Moksy limits abuse of its messaging routes
not: apply one global cap shared by every user

cards.subject: The Moksy in-memory limiter gap
says: is a known risk because the limiter counts per process
needs a Redis-backed limiter once several replicas run
cards.use: are asked why the current Moksy limiter would be inaccurate across several replicas
not: is already solved by a shared store

cards.subject: The Moksy reply-to token gap
says: is a known risk because the form thread plus an id can be enumerated
is to be fixed by signing the token with an HMAC
cards.use: are asked why Moksy plans to sign its reply-to tokens
not: is already fixed with a signature

cards.subject: Moksy thread controls
says: include per-thread mute, pin and mark-unread
let users decide which conversations alert them
cards.use: ask which conversation controls the Moksy communications service lists as done
not: are limited to delete and forward

cards.subject: Moksy read receipts
says: show in real time when a message has been read
come with aggregated unread counts
cards.use: ask how Moksy lets senders see a message was read
not: are sent by email once a day

cards.subject: Moksy planned token alerts
says: are planned to fire at 80, 90 and 100 percent of the allowance
warn a customer before running out
cards.use: ask when the Moksy token plan intends to warn about the allowance
not: are planned to fire only when the allowance is exhausted

cards.subject: The ggmoney email feature
says: sends payslips, invoices and deadline alerts through SendGrid
works but needs a verified sender
cards.use: ask what the ggmoney email feature needs before it can send
not: sends marketing newsletters through its own mail server

qa.q: What is the main difference between transactional and marketing email?
qa.right: Transactional email is triggered by a user's own action, while marketing email promotes to a consenting list
wrong: Transactional email is always plain text and marketing is always HTML
Marketing email is sent faster than transactional email
Transactional email always needs an unsubscribe link and marketing never does
qa.why: Transactional mail responds to an action or account event; marketing needs consent and an unsubscribe.

qa.q: Which DNS record type normally holds an SPF policy?
qa.right: TXT
qa.why: SPF is published as a TXT record.

qa.q: Which control lets a receiver confirm that a message body was not altered in transit?
qa.right: DKIM
qa.why: DKIM signs the message so alteration breaks the signature.

qa.q: What does a hard bounce mean?
qa.right: The address permanently cannot receive mail, for example because the mailbox does not exist
wrong: The recipient marked the message as spam
The message was opened but not clicked
qa.why: Hard bounces are permanent and the address should be suppressed.

qa.q: What should happen to an address that hard bounces?
qa.right: It should be added to the suppression list so it is not mailed again
wrong: It should be retried every hour for a week
It should be moved to the marketing list
It should be emailed from a different domain
qa.why: Repeated sends to dead addresses damage reputation.

qa.q: Which of these needs a working unsubscribe link?
qa.right: A product announcement sent to a newsletter list
wrong: A security alert about a new sign-in
qa.why: Marketing mail needs an unsubscribe; service messages do not.

qa.q: What is the purpose of the plain-text part of an email?
qa.right: It gives a readable version for clients that cannot or do not render HTML
wrong: It stores the tracking data for opens
qa.why: A text part improves compatibility and trust.

qa.q: What does alt text do for an image in an email?
qa.right: It describes the image for screen readers and when images are blocked
wrong: It makes the image load faster
It links the image to a web page
qa.why: Alt text is a text equivalent of the image.

qa.q: Why is it bad to send every notification inline during the user's own request?
qa.right: A slow or failing provider then slows or fails the user's action, and a crash can lose the message
qa.why: Storing first and delivering from a worker decouples the two.

qa.q: What does the outbox pattern guarantee when combined with retries?
qa.right: At-least-once delivery, so receivers must tolerate duplicates
wrong: Exactly-once delivery with no extra work
qa.why: Retries can repeat a send, so idempotency is needed.

qa.q: Which error type should a retry with backoff treat as temporary?
qa.right: A timeout or a rate-limit response from the provider
wrong: A response saying the recipient address is invalid
A response saying the sender domain is blocked by policy
A response saying the template does not exist
qa.why: Timeouts and rate limits may clear; invalid addresses will not.

qa.q: What is the purpose of jitter added to retry delays?
qa.right: To stop many workers retrying at the same instant
wrong: To make retries slower for ever
To increase the number of attempts
qa.why: Randomising delays spreads the load.

qa.q: What does the From domain in a DMARC check have to align with?
qa.right: The domain authenticated by SPF or DKIM
wrong: The domain of the provider's website
The domain in the Reply-To header
qa.why: DMARC requires aligned authentication for the visible From domain.

qa.q: Which action is a sensible first step when first publishing DMARC?
qa.right: Publish p=none with a report address and review who sends as the domain
wrong: Publish no record until spam appears
Remove SPF and rely on DMARC alone
qa.why: Monitoring mode reveals legitimate senders before enforcement.

qa.q: A webhook endpoint receives the same bounce event twice. What protects against processing it twice?
qa.right: Recording the provider's message or event id and ignoring ones already seen
wrong: Increasing the timeout on the endpoint
Sending a second bounce to the provider
qa.why: Idempotent handling by provider id is the standard defence.

qa.q: What should be done before a webhook endpoint trusts an incoming event?
qa.right: Verify the provider's signature or shared secret
wrong: Check that the request came over HTTP
Check that the body is under one kilobyte
Check that the user agent contains the provider's name
qa.why: Public URLs can be called by anyone, so authenticity must be proven.

qa.q: Why keep transactional and marketing mail on separate subdomains or streams?
qa.right: A marketing complaint spike then cannot block receipts and password resets
wrong: It removes the need for an unsubscribe link
qa.why: Reputation is tracked per domain and stream.

qa.q: What is IP warm-up?
qa.right: Raising the sending volume gradually on a new IP so providers learn the sender's pattern
wrong: Pinging an IP before mailing it
Switching on a dedicated IP at full volume
qa.why: New IPs have no reputation and need a slow ramp.

qa.q: Which header lets mail clients show a native unsubscribe button?
qa.right: List-Unsubscribe
qa.why: List-Unsubscribe carries a mailto or https address.

qa.q: What does the STOP keyword do in SMS marketing?
qa.right: Lets the recipient opt out by replying, and the sender must then stop marketing texts
qa.why: STOP is the standard opt-out and must be honoured.

qa.q: Which channel suits a low-urgency update that can wait until the next visit?
qa.right: An in-app notification
qa.why: Match channel intrusion to urgency.

qa.q: Why does an email log record often hold a provider message id?
qa.right: So later delivery events can be matched to the original send
wrong: So the message can be sent twice
qa.why: The id is the link between your record and the provider's events.

qa.q: Why are open rates an unreliable measure?
qa.right: Some clients preload images, which registers an open without the person reading
wrong: Only text emails can be opened
Opens are counted only after a reply
qa.why: Tracking pixels fire on image load, not on reading.

qa.q: Which practice helps a screen reader user choose links from a list?
qa.right: Descriptive link text such as View your invoice
wrong: Using the bare word here as every label
Using only an image as the link
Making all links the same colour
qa.why: Link text should make sense out of context.

qa.q: What is the safest way to test email sending in a staging environment holding real customer data?
qa.right: Use a recipient allow-list or a mail catcher so nothing reaches real customers
wrong: Send to real customers at night
Reduce the batch size to ten customers
qa.why: Staging must be unable to reach real customers.

qa.q: What should a good alert message contain?
qa.right: What happened, what the person should do and who to contact
wrong: A long history of the system
qa.why: Actionable messages cut follow-up tickets.

qa.q: What is the correct way to put a customer's name into an HTML email template?
qa.right: Escape it as text when it is inserted
wrong: Paste it in raw so formatting is kept
Put it only in the subject
qa.why: Unescaped user data can inject markup.

qa.q: What does a spam trap hit usually indicate?
qa.right: The list contains stale or illegitimately obtained addresses
wrong: The subject line is too long
The recipient clicked a link twice
qa.why: Traps catch poor list sourcing and hygiene.

qa.q: A team sees SPF pass for their provider's bounce domain, yet DMARC fails for their From domain. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: The SPF-authenticated domain does not align with the From domain and DKIM is not aligned either
qa.why: DMARC needs an aligned SPF or aligned DKIM result; passing SPF on another domain is not enough.

qa.q: A newsletter send is followed by a spike in spam complaints and the password reset emails start landing in spam. What should the team do first?
qa.right: Pause the campaign, check complaints and recipients, and move transactional mail to a separate stream
wrong: Resend the password resets more often
Switch every message to plain text
qa.why: Containing the problem and separating streams protects critical mail.

qa.q: A developer wants to add a 20 percent discount banner to every receipt email. What is the best reaction?
qa.right: Check whether promotional content changes the message's status and consent needs before adding it
wrong: Add it, since receipts are always exempt
Add it and remove the unsubscribe link
Add it only to the plain-text version
qa.why: Promotional content in a service message can bring it under marketing rules.

qa.q: A customer says they never received a password reset email. What should support check first?
qa.right: The email log for the message's status, then bounce or suppression entries for the address
wrong: Change the customer's password to a default
Ask the customer to reinstall the app
qa.why: The log shows whether it was sent, delivered or suppressed.

qa.q: A new IP is configured and the team plans to send the full 500,000 contact list on day one. What is the best advice?
qa.right: Warm up the IP, starting with the most engaged contacts and increasing volume
wrong: Send the full list; volume proves the IP is good
Split the list into alphabetical order
qa.why: Reputation must be built gradually.

qa.q: A team imports an old list bought from a third party and sends a campaign. Soon bounces and trap hits rise. What went wrong?
qa.right: The list had no consent or hygiene, so it hurt reputation
wrong: The subject line was too short
The HTML had too many tables
The DNS TTL was too long
qa.why: Unverified purchased lists produce bounces and spam trap hits.

qa.q: A provider starts returning rate-limit errors during a burst of 10,000 notifications. What is the best design response?
qa.right: Queue the messages and retry with backoff at a paced rate
wrong: Retry every message immediately in a loop
qa.why: A queue with backoff smooths bursts without losing messages.

qa.q: A worker crashes after the database commit but before calling the email provider. Which design avoids losing the message?
qa.right: Storing it in an outbox that a worker drains and retries
wrong: Sending the message twice to be safe
qa.why: A durable outbox survives a crash between save and send.

qa.q: Your outbox retries a message after a timeout, and the first attempt had actually succeeded. How do you avoid a duplicate email?
qa.right: Send with an idempotency key so the repeat is recognised
wrong: Lower the timeout to one second
Delete the record after the first try
qa.why: Retries of an ambiguous attempt need idempotency.

qa.q: An item has failed after its maximum retries. What should happen to it?
qa.right: It moves to a dead state where a person can inspect it
qa.why: Dead items need human attention, not silent loops.

qa.q: An incident is affecting many customers and the cause is not yet known. What is the best customer message?
qa.right: State the impact, what is being investigated and when the next update will come
wrong: Say it will be fixed within an hour
Say nothing until the cause is known
qa.why: Honest scope and a cadence beat guessed timelines.

qa.q: A customer replies to a message from no-reply and gets no answer. What should change?
qa.right: Use a monitored reply address or tell the customer clearly where to get help
qa.why: Replies should go somewhere a person looks.

qa.q: A developer logs the full password reset URL when a reset email is sent. What is wrong?
qa.right: The log now holds a live credential that anyone with log access could use
wrong: Reset URLs are too long to log
Logs must be in JSON only
qa.why: Secrets and tokens should be redacted or never logged.

qa.q: A team finds the same disk-full alert has produced 400 emails overnight. Which feature should they add?
qa.right: Alert deduplication with a key for resource and condition
qa.why: Deduplication collapses repeats of the same underlying issue.

qa.q: A user turns off all marketing mail but still receives a new sign-in alert. Is this correct?
qa.right: Yes, security alerts are service messages and are sent regardless of marketing preferences
wrong: No, an opt-out must stop every email
Yes, but only if the alert contains a discount
No, the alert must be sent by SMS instead
qa.why: Security and account messages are separate from marketing consent.

qa.q: A contact form places the visitor's input directly in the Subject header. What attack is possible?
qa.right: Header injection, where line breaks add extra recipients or headers
wrong: Cross-site request forgery on the logo
qa.why: Newlines in header values let attackers add headers.

qa.q: A team wants to send a legal notice and prove later that the customer was notified. What should they keep?
qa.right: An append-only audit record with recipient, time, template version and delivery status
wrong: A copy of the SMTP password
qa.why: An audit trail with the template version reproduces what was sent.

qa.q: A monthly summary is being sent as 30 separate notifications to heavy users who then mute everything. What is the better design?
qa.right: Batch the low-urgency events into a digest
wrong: Raise the volume of each message
qa.why: A digest lowers volume for non-urgent events.

qa.q: A DMARC aggregate report shows an unfamiliar source passing SPF but failing alignment. What is a sensible next step?
qa.right: Find out whether it is a forgotten legitimate sender, and fix it before moving toward enforcement
qa.why: Reports reveal unknown senders to deal with before enforcing.

qa.q: A team moves from p=none to p=reject in one step and customer invoices from a third-party billing tool start bouncing. What was missed?
qa.right: Checking that every legitimate third-party sender passes DMARC before enforcing
qa.why: Enforcement without covering third-party senders blocks real mail.

qa.q: Your queue depth rises steadily for an hour but the dead count is zero. What does this suggest?
qa.right: Messages are created faster than they can be sent, such as from rate limiting or slow delivery
qa.why: Rising depth without dead items shows backlog, not failure.

qa.q: A provider outage lasts 20 minutes. Which design keeps most notifications from being lost?
qa.right: An outbox with retries and backoff that delivers after the provider recovers
wrong: Calling another API with the same data
qa.why: Durable storage and backoff cover short outages.

qa.q: A reviewer says a reset email says 'No account found for that address'. What is the privacy problem?
qa.right: It reveals which addresses have accounts; use a neutral message either way
wrong: It does not include a logo
qa.why: Neutral responses avoid account enumeration.

qa.q: This record is published for example.com. What does it do?
qa.right: It lists the servers allowed to send for the domain and tells receivers to treat others as failing hard
wrong: It signs each message with a private key
It tells receivers where to send reports
qa.why: An SPF record lists permitted senders; -all marks others as hard fail.

qa.q: What does p=quarantine mean in this record?
qa.right: Failing mail should be treated as suspicious, typically sent to spam, and reports go to the address given
wrong: Failing mail should be ignored with no reports
Passing mail should be held for review
qa.why: quarantine sits between none and reject; rua names the report address.

qa.q: What do the two headers below allow a mail client to do?
qa.right: Offer a one-click unsubscribe button that sends a POST request
qa.why: List-Unsubscribe plus List-Unsubscribe-Post enables one-click unsubscribe.

qa.q: What is wrong with this retry loop?
qa.right: It retries instantly with no delay and no limit, hammering a failing provider forever
wrong: It uses the wrong HTTP method
qa.why: Retries need backoff and a maximum number of attempts.

qa.q: Which change makes this retry safer?
qa.right: Add a maximum attempts count and wait longer between attempts
wrong: Send the message twice per loop
Run the loop on the main thread
qa.why: Backoff and an attempt cap prevent runaway retries.

qa.q: What is wrong with building this subject line?
qa.right: User input containing a line break could add extra headers
qa.why: Strip CR and LF from any value placed in a header.

qa.q: What does the multipart structure below provide?
qa.right: Text and HTML versions of one message, from which the client chooses
wrong: Two separate emails to the same person
An attachment and a calendar invite
qa.why: multipart/alternative holds equivalent versions.
qa.code:
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; boundary="b1" --b1 Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 Hello --b1 Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Hello

--b1--

qa.q: A marketing manager wants to use a 'Last chance! Ends in 1 hour!' banner on every weekly email, though no deadline exists. Why push back?
qa.right: False urgency erodes trust and teaches people to ignore real alerts
wrong: Banners increase spam scores in every case
Deadlines are not allowed in email
qa.why: Honest urgency preserves the value of real alerts.

qa.q: A team wants to count how many customers read each invoice email using a tracking pixel. What caveat applies?
qa.right: Opens can be inflated by image preloading, so it is not a reliable proof of reading
wrong: Pixels cannot be added to HTML
Pixels only work on plain text
qa.why: Treat opens as a rough signal, not evidence.
